name: Posterior ankle impingement
populations: people with an os trigonum or a prominent lateral talar process
summary: Posterior ankle pain in forced plantarflexion as the posterior talar process or os trigonum, capsule and soft tissue are squeezed between the tibia and calcaneus, typical in dancers and footballers.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Forced or repeated plantarflexion: en pointe or demi-pointe, kicking, push-off, downhill running

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; in one small series 60% improved without surgery and 40% needed excision

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior pain reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion; diagnosis is mainly clinical

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral radiograph in maximal plantarflexion shows an os trigonum or posterior process; MRI shows soft tissue and oedema

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Full activity after arthroscopic excision averaged 11.3 weeks versus 16.0 weeks after open surgery

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No population estimate found; dance accounts for 62% of sports cases reported in one review

overview:
Posterior ankle impingement syndrome is a clinical disorder with posterior ankle pain that occurs in forced plantarflexion. The pain can be acute after trauma or chronic from repetitive stress. Pathology of the os trigonum and posterior talar process is the most common cause, but flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tenosynovitis, ankle osteochondritis, subtalar joint disease and fracture can also cause it [r1]. When the os trigonum is the main problem it is called os trigonum syndrome, an overuse injury seen mostly in ballet dancers and soccer players [r2].

Both bone and soft tissue are involved. In ballet, the en pointe and demi-pointe positions of maximal plantarflexion put excessive force on the posterior ankle [r3]. Treatment starts with non-surgical care, and surgery is used for refractory cases [r1,r2]. The evidence is weak: it is confined to Level IV and V studies, and there are no prospective studies on the natural history or on outcomes of conservative treatment [r4].

epidemiology.text: No population incidence or prevalence of posterior ankle impingement was found in the sources reviewed, so none is quoted here. A review of management in sport found that dance dominates the literature, accounting for 62% of the reported sports [r4]. The syndrome is described in ballet dancers, soccer players and downhill runners, who report pain at the posterolateral aspect of the talus [r5,r2]. Overuse injuries are typical in dancers and downhill runners, whereas trauma can produce an acute form after hyperplantarflexion or a combined inversion and plantarflexion injury [r5].

intrinsic: An os trigonum or a protruding (prolonged) lateral talar process, two common anatomical variations linked to posterior impingement in ballet dancers [r3]
A large range of ankle plantarflexion, as required of dancers en pointe and demi-pointe [r3]
Coexisting FHL tendon pathology, which often accompanies os trigonum syndrome [r2]
Previous trauma such as hyperplantarflexion or an inversion–plantarflexion ankle injury [r5]
extrinsic: Repetitive end-range plantarflexion: en pointe and demi-pointe work, kicking, push-off and downhill running [r1,r2]
Participation in dance, where the demands on plantarflexion are unavoidable [r4,r6]
High volumes of jumping and relevé work without adequate recovery (clinical reasoning)

mechanism.summary: Forced plantarflexion closes the gap between the back of the tibia and the top of the calcaneus. In dancers en pointe, MRI showed the posterior edge of the tibial plafond, the posterior talus and the superior calcaneus converging in all nine dancers scanned [r7]. The posterior talar process, an os trigonum if present, and the soft tissue behind them are compressed between these bones [r2,r3]. Repeated loading in dancers, footballers and downhill runners, or a single hyperplantarflexion or inversion–plantarflexion injury, produces pain, swelling and sometimes fracture [r5,r1].
sequence: The athlete moves into end-range plantarflexion: a dancer rises en pointe or demi-pointe, a footballer kicks or pushes off, or a runner descends a slope [r1,r2].
The ankle plantarflexes until the posterior tibial lip, the posterior talus and the calcaneus converge [r7].
The os trigonum or the posterior talar process is caught between the tibia and the calcaneus, and the posterior capsule and soft tissue are squeezed [r2,r8].
Repeated compression irritates the capsule and synovium, causes soft tissue thickening and can stress or fracture the posterior process or the os trigonum [r9,r5].
The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs behind the talus and is often involved, with stenosing tenosynovitis in dancers [r10,r2].
Posterior ankle pain develops at the end of plantarflexion and limits pointing, push-off and kicking [r2].
If the athlete keeps loading the joint, pain becomes persistent, and non-surgical care may fail [r4].

variants.name: Acute traumatic
variants.description: A single hyperplantarflexion injury or a combined inversion–plantarflexion injury, which can fracture the os trigonum or the posterior process [r5,r9].

variants.name: Chronic overuse (dancers, footballers, downhill runners)
variants.description: Repetitive plantarflexion stress, with posterolateral talar tenderness [r5,r2].

variants.name: Osseous: os trigonum or prominent lateral talar process
variants.description: The os trigonum and a protruding lateral talar process are the two commonest anatomical variations associated with impingement in ballet dancers [r3].

variants.name: Soft tissue: posterolateral capsule or scar
variants.description: Without an ossicle, MRI may show scar tissue behind the posterior talus, with similar symptoms [r2]. Capsule abnormalities were treated with ultrasound-guided injection in elite soccer players [r8].

variants.name: With FHL tenosynovitis
variants.description: Combined bony impingement and FHL tendon pathology is common and changes the surgical plan [r5,r2].

anatomy.text: The posterior talus has a lateral and a medial tubercle with the FHL tendon running in a groove between them. The lateral tubercle can be prolonged (Stieda process), or a separate ossicle, the os trigonum, can lie behind the talus. The posterior talofibular ligament attaches to the lateral tubercle. In maximal plantarflexion these structures sit between the posterior tibial lip and the calcaneus, where an os trigonum is seen on a lateral radiograph [r2]. The posterior capsule, synovium and the FHL tendon sheath lie in the same space [r8,r5].

structures.name: Posterior talar process (lateral tubercle) and os trigonum
structures.role: Bony prominence or ossicle behind the talus that is compressed between tibia and calcaneus in plantarflexion [r2]

structures.name: Posterior tibial lip
structures.role: Posterior edge of the distal tibia that closes down on the talus in plantarflexion [r7]

structures.name: Posterolateral capsule and synovium
structures.role: Soft tissue that can thicken, scar or become inflamed. Abnormality here is a target for injection [r8].

structures.name: Flexor hallucis longus tendon
structures.role: Runs in the groove behind the talus and often becomes tenosynovitic with posterior impingement [r2,r10]

structures.name: Posterior talofibular ligament
structures.role: Attaches to the lateral tubercle and can be involved with the posterior process

structures.name: Calcaneus (superior surface)
structures.role: Closes up toward the tibia in plantarflexion [r7]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In forced plantarflexion, bone and soft tissue behind the talus are compressed. Pathology of the os trigonum and the posterior talar process is the most common cause, although FHL tenosynovitis, osteochondritis, subtalar disease and fracture can also cause pain [r1]. In ballet dancers, the extreme plantarflexion of en pointe and demi-pointe places excessive force on the posterior ankle and can lead to impingement, pain and disability, and conditions of both bony and soft tissue origin are recognised [r3]. A radiograph in a series of 30 cases showed an os trigonum or posterior process fracture in 63%, and an intact posterior process in 33% [r9].

Imaging findings do not always explain symptoms. In a small MRI study of nine dancers en pointe, convergence of the bones was found in all of them, and Stieda's process and anterior spurs were each seen in 44%, but the clinical signs did not always correlate with the pain reported [r7]. Soft tissue scar behind the talus can produce the same symptoms as an os trigonum [r2].

structures.name: Os trigonum or posterior talar process
structures.effect: Compressed, stressed or fractured. Present on radiographs in a large share of symptomatic cases [r9]

structures.name: Posterior capsule and synovium
structures.effect: Pinched, inflamed and thickened, with scar tissue behind the talus on MRI in some cases [r2,r8]

structures.name: FHL tendon
structures.effect: Stenosing tenosynovitis often coexists. Of 41 operations in 37 dancers, 26 were for tendinitis and posterior impingement, 9 for tendinitis alone and 6 for impingement alone [r10].

structures.name: Posterior tibial lip and calcaneus
structures.effect: Converge on the posterior talus at end-range plantarflexion [r7]

structures.name: Joint cartilage and synovium
structures.effect: Synovitis and effusion were seen in 67% of dancers on MRI [r7]

muscles.name: Flexor hallucis longus
muscles.effect: Tenosynovitis and pain on resisted great-toe flexion; frequent in dancers [r10,r2]

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles.effect: Repetitive plantarflexion loading in dance, kicking and push-off, and guarding after injury (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Peroneals and deep foot muscles
muscles.effect: May overwork to control the ankle and foot at end range in dancers (clinical reasoning)

cellular.description: Repeated compression irritates the posterior capsule and synovium, with pain and swelling at the end of plantarflexion [r2,r7].
Soft tissue behind the posterior talus can thicken or scar, producing symptoms without an ossicle [r2].
The os trigonum or posterior process may be stressed, or fractured after hyperplantarflexion trauma [r5,r9].
The FHL sheath becomes tenosynovitic with repetitive plantarflexion and great-toe flexion [r10,r2].

systems.effect: Pain at the end of plantarflexion drives avoidance of pointing and push-off, with altered technique (clinical reasoning). Nerve compression at the tarsal tunnel is part of the differential [r1].
Synovitis and effusion accompany the compression, and may respond to injection [r7,r8].
Dancers and footballers compensate with altered ankle, foot and hip strategies (clinical reasoning).
Dancers and professional athletes face performance and career pressure, which influences return to activity. Outcomes after surgery differed between professional and amateur dancers [r10].

grading.system: Descriptive classification by dominant pathology (no validated grading)

grades.description: Os trigonum, prolonged lateral talar process (Stieda), or fracture of the posterior process [r3,r9].
grades.prognosis: Non-operative care first. In one small series, 60% of followed cases improved without surgery and 40% needed excision [r9].

grades.description: Posterior capsule thickening, scar or synovitis without an ossicle [r2,r8].
grades.prognosis: Often treated non-operatively; injection and arthroscopic debridement have been used (Level IV evidence) [r8,r4]

grades.description: Bony or soft tissue impingement plus FHL tendon pathology [r5,r10].
grades.prognosis: Surgery may involve simultaneous FHL release. In dancers, 30 of 40 operations had good or excellent results [r10].

timeframes.summary: There are no prospective data on the natural history or on conservative outcomes [r4]. Symptoms typically improve with non-surgical management, and surgery is used in refractory cases [r1]. After surgery, time to full activity averaged 11.3 weeks after endoscopic and 16.0 weeks after open excision in a systematic review of Level IV studies [r11].

healing.description: Activity modification can settle capsular and tendon irritation in some patients [r2]
Progressive strength, plantarflexion tolerance and sport-specific loading (clinical convention)
Full activity at an average of 11.3 weeks in a systematic review [r11]
Full activity at an average of 16.0 weeks in the same review [r11]

milestones.label: Conservative trial
milestones.note: A trial of 6–12 weeks of activity modification and rehabilitation is a common convention; 60% improved without surgery in one small series [r9]

milestones.label: Return in soccer versus dance
milestones.note: Soccer players return more quickly than dancers [r4]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, not time-based. With non-surgical care, return as pain-free end-range plantarflexion allows. After arthroscopic excision, the average time to full activity was 11.3 weeks, compared with 16.0 weeks after open excision [r11]. Soccer players appear to return more quickly than dancers, and arthro-endoscopic surgery allows earlier return [r4]. Follow the surgeon's protocol.

symptoms: Deep posterior ankle pain, often posterolateral, brought on by plantarflexion [r1,r5]
Pain when going up on the toes (relevé), en pointe, pushing off, kicking or running downhill [r1,r2]
Chronic or recurrent pain, or an acute onset after a hyperplantarflexion or inversion–plantarflexion injury [r1,r5]
Posterior swelling or stiffness, and sometimes pain or catching along the great toe tendon (FHL) [r10]
Reduced ability to point the foot or push off at full strength
signs: Tenderness at the posterolateral aspect of the talus, behind the peroneal tendons and lateral to the Achilles [r5]
Pain reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion [r1]
Pain or crepitus along the FHL tendon on great-toe flexion or extension (clinical reasoning) [r10]
Normal or minimally reduced dorsiflexion with limited painful plantarflexion

subjective: Pain location (posterolateral, posteromedial or along the heel) and the movements that provoke it: relevé, en pointe, kicking, push-off, downhill running [r1]
Acute event: hyperplantarflexion or an inversion–plantarflexion injury, and whether the athlete could weight-bear [r5]
Training load, dance schedule, type of shoes and the proportion of time en pointe or demi-pointe
Previous ankle sprains and previous treatment
Great-toe pain or triggering, which suggests FHL involvement [r2]
Professional or amateur status and the timing of competition, because it affects decisions on surgery [r10]
observation: Dance or kicking technique, and the position at the end of plantarflexion
palpation: Posterolateral talus, between the peroneal tendons and Achilles tendon [r5]
FHL tendon behind the medial malleolus and along its groove
Achilles tendon and its insertion, retrocalcaneal area
Peroneal and posterior tibial tendons; tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel (differential) [r1]
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive plantarflexion, compared with the other side
Pain at end-range passive plantarflexion with gentle overpressure [r1]
Dorsiflexion, subtalar motion and great-toe extension
strength: Calf capacity (single-leg heel raises to the height required)
Peroneal and deep foot muscle strength
Hip and trunk control for the sport
neuro: Tibial and sural nerve sensation and Tinel's sign at the tarsal tunnel (to exclude tarsal tunnel syndrome) [r1]
functional: Single-leg relevé or heel raise to full height, then demi-pointe or pointe for dancers [r3]
Kicking technique and volume in footballers

specialTests.name: Forced passive plantarflexion test (posterior impingement test)
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce posterior ankle pain by compressing the posterior talus
specialTests.procedure: Patient seated or supine with the knee flexed. Passively plantarflex the ankle to the end of range with gentle repeated overpressure, or briefly sustained, comparing sides.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the patient's deep posterior or posterolateral pain, with a firm end-feel [r1]

specialTests.name: Resisted great-toe flexion with the ankle plantarflexed (FHL test)
specialTests.purpose: Identify flexor hallucis longus tenosynovitis, which often coexists
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the FHL behind the medial malleolus and in its groove while the patient actively flexes and extends the great toe, with the ankle in plantarflexion and dorsiflexion.
specialTests.positive: Pain, crepitus or triggering along the tendon, with posterior pain on great-toe motion [r10,r2]

specialTests.name: Weight-bearing relevé or demi-pointe reproduction
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce the provocative functional position for the dancer or athlete
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to rise to the height at which pain begins, then to their full relevé or demi-pointe, and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of posterior pain at the end of rise, or inability to reach the required height [r2]

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa ankle rules (for acute injury)
clinicalRules.description: After an acute hyperplantarflexion or inversion injury, use the Ottawa ankle rules and a low threshold for radiographs, because a posterior process fracture can present as ankle sprain [r9].

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM)
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported function and sport; baseline and follow-up

outcomeMeasures.name: Numerical pain rating at end-range plantarflexion tasks
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain at relevé, push-off or kicking

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg heel-raise endurance
outcomeMeasures.use: Functional calf capacity; compare with the other side

outcomeMeasures.name: Plantarflexion range of motion
outcomeMeasures.use: Goniometric range, and pain onset angle

imaging.indication: First-line imaging for suspected posterior impingement
imaging.findings: An os trigonum typically lies between the posterior tibial lip and the calcaneus [r2]. In a series of 30 cases, an os trigonum or posterior process fracture was seen in 63% and an intact posterior process in 33% [r9].

imaging.indication: No ossicle on radiograph, suspected soft tissue or FHL involvement, or planning for surgery
imaging.findings: Scar tissue behind the posterior talus, bone and soft tissue oedema, synovitis and FHL tenosynovitis [r2,r12]. Findings do not always match symptoms, because clinical signs did not always correlate with reported pain in dancers [r7].

imaging.indication: Posterolateral capsule abnormality in athletes, and for guided injection
imaging.findings: Used to guide steroid and anaesthetic injection into a posterolateral capsule abnormality in elite soccer players [r8]

imaging.indication: Surgical planning, or doubt about a fracture of the posterior process
imaging.findings: Defines the bony anatomy of the os trigonum and posterior process (clinical convention); radiography, scintigraphy, CT and MRI depict bone and soft tissue abnormalities [r1]

differentials.name: Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or tenosynovitis
differentials.distinguishing: Pain behind the medial malleolus and along the FHL groove with great-toe motion; often coexists with posterior impingement [r10,r2]

differentials.name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the Achilles insertion or in the retrocalcaneal region, worse on loading in dorsiflexion and on palpation of the tendon, not at the posterolateral talus

differentials.name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Burning or numbness over the plantar foot, positive Tinel's sign behind the medial malleolus. Nerve compression is part of the differential [r1].

differentials.name: Osteochondral lesion of the talus
differentials.distinguishing: Deep ankle pain with catching or swelling; posteromedial dome lesions can mimic posterior pain. MRI or CT confirms. Ankle osteochondritis is a recognised cause of posterior pain [r1].

differentials.name: Lateral ankle sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Inversion injury with lateral ligament tenderness, though posterior pain after inversion–plantarflexion injury can reflect impingement [r5]

differentials.name: Anterior ankle impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior pain at end-range dorsiflexion, rather than posterior pain in plantarflexion

differentials.name: Subtalar joint disease or fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Hindfoot pain with inversion and eversion, and abnormal subtalar imaging. Subtalar disease and fracture can also cause posterior ankle pain [r1].

differentials.name: Achilles tendon rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden posterior calf or ankle pain with a palpable gap, weak plantarflexion and a positive Thompson test

redFlags: A hyperplantarflexion or inversion injury with severe pain, bony tenderness or inability to weight-bear: arrange radiographs to look for a fracture of the posterior process or os trigonum [r9].
A palpable gap, a positive Thompson test or sudden weakness of plantarflexion: suspect Achilles tendon rupture and refer urgently.
Burning, numbness or tingling over the sole of the foot, or a positive Tinel's sign at the tarsal tunnel: consider nerve compression and refer if neurological signs progress [r1].
Night or rest pain, fever, a hot swollen ankle or unexplained weight loss: consider infection, inflammatory arthropathy or tumour, and arrange urgent medical review.
Persistent posterior pain despite a thorough conservative trial: refer to an orthopaedic foot and ankle specialist for imaging and consideration of excision [r1,r2].

After surgery: wound problems, severe pain, a cold or numb foot, or calf swelling need urgent review. Complications were 3.9% for open medial, 12.7% for open lateral and 4.8% for arthro-endoscopic surgery in one review [r4].

management.principles: Start with non-surgical management and escalate to surgery only for refractory cases [r1,r2]. Non-surgical care centres on activity modification, graded rehabilitation and treatment of coexisting FHL and capsular irritation. The evidence is limited: it is confined to Level IV and V studies, and there are no prospective studies of the natural history or of conservative treatment outcomes [r4]. In the best available small series, 60% of the 20 cases followed improved with non-operative treatment, and 40% needed excision [r9]. Surgery gives good results in most patients, and endoscopic techniques have lower complication rates and a faster return to full activity than open procedures in a systematic review of Level IV studies [r11]. Decisions should be shared with the dancer or athlete and consider the demands of their sport, since dancers may be unable to avoid plantarflexion [r2].

medical.name: Ultrasound-guided steroid and anaesthetic injection into a posterolateral capsule abnormality
medical.description: Reported in elite soccer players with clinical posterior impingement and a posterolateral capsule abnormality on MRI. It was well tolerated and allowed a rapid return to athletic activity in all patients, but the study was small and uncontrolled, and specific numbers were not given in the abstract [r8].

medical.name: Surgical excision of the os trigonum or posterior process (endoscopic or open)
medical.description: For refractory cases [r1,r2]. In a systematic review of 16 studies, endoscopic surgery had a lower complication rate (7.2% vs 15.9%) and a shorter time to full activity (11.3 vs 16.0 weeks) than open surgery, but all the studies were Level IV [r11]. A review of 905 procedures found that 81% required excision of bone, complication rates were 3.9% for open medial, 12.7% for open lateral and 4.8% for arthro-endoscopic surgery, and there was no evidence of superior long-term results for either technique [r4]. Endoscopic management gives good or excellent results in about 80% of patients at 2–5 years [r5].

medical.name: FHL release for coexisting tenosynovitis
medical.description: Performed with excision when bony impingement and FHL tendinopathy coexist [r5]. In 37 dancers (41 operations), 30 had a good or excellent result, 6 fair and 4 poor, after a mean follow-up of 7 years. Results were good or excellent in 28 of 34 ankles in professional dancers but only 2 of 6 in amateurs [r10].

medical.name: Short-term analgesia, anti-inflammatory medication or a period of protection
medical.description: Used for a flare. Reviews describe conservative therapy with immobilisation, physical therapy and activity cessation in dancers [r6]. No trials of medication were identified.

physio.name: Activity modification and load management
physio.description: Symptoms may improve with rest or activity modification, particularly by reducing plantarflexion at end range (en pointe or demi-pointe time, kicking and push-off volume, downhill running) [r2]. Keep the athlete training in other ways.

physio.name: Graded strength and control program (calf, FHL, foot, hip, trunk)
physio.description: Physical therapy forms part of non-surgical treatment [r2]. Rebuild calf and FHL capacity, foot intrinsic strength and proximal control, then progress relevé, hopping and sport-specific loading.

physio.name: Technique review in dancers and footballers
physio.description: Work with the dance teacher or coach on the demands and volume of end-range plantarflexion. Dance reviews note that plantarflexion cannot always be avoided, which is why dancers may need surgery [r2,r6].

physio.name: Soft tissue treatment for the calf and FHL
physio.description: Manual therapy to the calf and FHL region may reduce symptoms by easing muscle tension, but no trials were identified in this condition.

physio.name: Post-operative rehabilitation
physio.description: Early mobilisation and graded strengthening under the surgeon's protocol. Average time to full activity was 11.3 weeks after endoscopic and 16.0 weeks after open surgery [r11].

physio.name: Forced end-range plantarflexion stretching or repeated pointing into pain
physio.description: Forcing plantarflexion reproduces the compression that causes the pain [r1]. Avoid it until pain settles, and use graded exposure instead (expert opinion based on the mechanism).

education: Pain at the back of the ankle when you point your foot is from tissue or a small bone being squeezed. It often settles with a change in load and a rehabilitation program.
An extra small bone (os trigonum) is common in the general population, and it does not always cause pain. Treatment is based on your symptoms, not on the scan alone [r7].
Avoid repeated forced pointing, kicking or push-off into pain, but keep your fitness and strength training going.
If a thorough trial of rehabilitation does not settle it, keyhole (arthroscopic) surgery to remove the bone or tissue is an option that has good results in most patients [r11].
Dancers and professional athletes should plan the timing of a return with their teacher, coach and medical team.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and driven by pain at end-range plantarflexion, swelling and function in the demands of the sport or dance. There are no prospective trials of non-operative treatment [r4], so the program below is built from reviews that recommend non-surgical care first and from clinical reasoning [r1,r2]. After surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol, expecting about 11–16 weeks to full activity [r11]. Dosages are common clinical conventions.

stages.name: Settle & protect
precautions: Exclude fracture after any acute hyperplantarflexion injury
Avoid pointing, en pointe, kicking and push-off into pain
Stop if night pain or neurological symptoms appear

exercises.name: Ankle alphabet within a pain-free range
exercises.cues: Stay out of the painful end of plantarflexion

exercises.name: Seated calf raise to a comfortable height
exercises.cues: Controlled rise and lower, stop before posterior pain

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and hold the pelvis level

exercises.name: Plank (core endurance)
exercises.cues: Neutral trunk and steady breathing

exercises.name: Cycling or pool work for fitness
exercises.cues: Keep the foot flat on the pedal, avoid pointing into pain

progressionCriteria: No increase in swelling after exercise
No posterior pain on gentle passive plantarflexion

stages.name: Restore range & strength
precautions: Keep plantarflexion below the pain-onset angle
No forced pointing or stretching into pain

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise (partial height)
exercises.cues: Rise only to the pain-free height

exercises.name: Band-resisted plantarflexion and eversion
exercises.cues: Move only at the ankle

exercises.name: Great-toe flexor strengthening (towel curls, resisted toe flexion)
exercises.cues: Keep the heel down and the movement smooth

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.cues: Soft knee, quiet ankle

exercises.name: Single-leg bridge
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level

progressionCriteria: Double-leg calf raise × 15 without posterior pain

stages.name: Capacity & end-range control
goals: Graded exposure to higher relevé or plantarflexion
precautions: Increase relevé height only if pain stays ≤ 3/10 and settles within 24 hours

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Slow lowering over 3 s

exercises.name: Graded relevé (demi-pointe holds) rising by 1–2 cm per week
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 holds of 3–5 s, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Keep the weight over the big toe and avoid sickling

exercises.name: Double-leg then single-leg hopping
exercises.cues: Soft landing

exercises.name: Walk–jog progression
exercises.dosage: 1–2 min jog intervals building to 20–30 min over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Short, quiet steps, avoid downhill initially

exercises.name: Single-leg squat
exercises.cues: Knee over second toe, level pelvis

progressionCriteria: Single-leg heel raise × 20 without posterior pain
Relevé or demi-pointe to the needed height without pain
Hop and landing tests without pain

stages.name: Return to dance or sport
goals: Return to full en pointe, kicking or push-off demands
precautions: Increase pointe work, kicking or downhill running volume in small steps
Re-assess if posterior pain or swelling recurs

exercises.name: Graded en pointe or demi-pointe work (dancers)
exercises.dosage: Start with 5–10 minutes at the barre and build over 3–4 weeks
exercises.cues: Quality technique and control into full relevé

exercises.name: Kicking program (footballers)
exercises.cues: Controlled contact and follow-through

exercises.name: Push-off and acceleration drills
exercises.cues: Drive through the big toe without pain

exercises.name: Jump-landing drills
exercises.cues: Land softly with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Maintenance calf, FHL and hip strength
exercises.cues: Keep heavy slow calf work in the program

progressionCriteria: Full participation in class, rehearsal or team training without posterior pain
Single-leg heel raise capacity about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Athlete or dancer confident at end-range plantarflexion

criteria: No validated return-to-sport criteria were identified for posterior ankle impingement. The criteria below are clinical conventions.
Pain-free end-range plantarflexion at the sport or dance demand: relevé, en pointe, kicking or push-off
No swelling or posterior pain after full training sessions
Single-leg heel raise and calf capacity within about 90% of the other side
FHL pain-free with great-toe flexion and in demi-pointe
Hop, landing and running tasks without pain
Agreement with the coach, dance teacher and medical team on the load progression

prognosis: No prospective natural-history data were found [r4]. In a small series of 30 cases, 20 were followed, and 12 (60%) improved with non-operative treatment while 8 (40%) required excision, with good to excellent results in 7 and fair in 1 of the operated cases [r9]. In 37 dancers (41 operations) followed for a mean of 7 years, 30 ankles had a good or excellent result, 6 fair and 4 poor, and results were better in professional than amateur dancers [r10]. Endoscopic management gave good or excellent results in about 80% of patients at 2–5 years [r5]. Soccer players return more quickly than dancers [r4].
prevention: No prevention studies were identified. The following points are clinical reasoning.
Build volume of en pointe, demi-pointe, kicking and downhill running gradually, with rest days (clinical reasoning).
Treat early posterior pain with load modification before it becomes chronic [r2].
Maintain calf, FHL, foot and hip strength and good technique, and restore ankle range after any ankle injury.
clinicalPearls: Diagnosis is mainly clinical: posterior pain in forced plantarflexion, posterolateral tenderness, and a lateral radiograph in plantarflexion to look for the os trigonum [r1,r2].
Imaging does not always match symptoms. In nine dancers en pointe, the MRI changes were frequent, but clinical signs did not always correlate with pain, so treat the patient and not the image [r7].
Always check the FHL. Os trigonum syndrome is often associated with FHL pathology, and most dancer operations in one series were for tendinitis with or without impingement [r2,r10].
Non-operative care is the first step. In a small series 60% of those followed improved without surgery, but there are no prospective trials [r9,r4].
If surgery is needed, endoscopic excision had fewer complications and a quicker return to full activity than open surgery in a systematic review of Level IV studies [r11].
Set expectations: dancers return more slowly than soccer players after surgery, and professional dancers did better than amateurs in one series [r4,r10].

captions.text: A ballet dancer repeats the relevé, rising to demi-pointe and en pointe, every rehearsal.
She rises onto the ball of the foot, the ankle plantarflexing towards its limit.
At the top, the back of the tibia and the calcaneus close down on the talus.
She lowers, then repeats the movement again and again.
With each repetition the tissue behind the ankle is compressed, and pain builds.
Zooming into the back of the right ankle, viewed from the lateral side.

actions.text: May stress or fracture with trauma

captions.text: Behind the talus lies the posterior talar process, sometimes with a separate bone, the os trigonum.
In full plantarflexion the back of the tibia and the top of the calcaneus close towards each other.
The bone and the soft tissue behind it are caught in the gap.
The capsule and synovium become inflamed and swollen.
Repeated loading, or one forced hyperplantarflexion, can stress or fracture the bone.
Deep pain at the back of the ankle follows when the dancer rises on her toes or pushes off.
Healthy posterior capsule and synovium: a thin, mobile lining.
Repeated compression inflames the synovium, with swelling and pain.
Fibrous tissue thickens the capsule behind the talus.
The thickened tissue takes up space and limits end-range plantarflexion.
Load modification, rehabilitation or excision lets the lining remodel and the range recover.
